{"id": "18:23/q13", "question": "How is the exception 'unless God wills' grammatically connected to this prohibition?", "turns_on": "Whether the exception qualifies the act of saying, the intended act, the kind of action, or the possibility of speaking at all; whether an omitted saying or preposition is needed.", "positions": [{"id": "18:23/q13/p1", "position": "An omitted verb of saying gives 'unless you say: if God wills'.", "reasons": "Al-Farrāʾ states this sense; al-Akhfash supplies 'say' in al-Māwardī, al-Wāḥidī, and al-Ṭabarasī. Al-Wāḥidī says brevity indicates the longer wording; al-Mubarrad, reporting al-Kisāʾī and al-Farrāʾ, says deletion shifts 'wills' to a future form. Ibn al-Jawzī also supplies the verb. Al-Ṭabarasī says it averts a false promise or broken oath. Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī objects that it strains the wording and changes the meaning."}, {"id": "18:23/q13/p2", "position": "It means one may state an intended action only by God's will, without inserting a verb of saying.", "reasons": "Al-Farrāʾ as reported by al-Ṭabarasī prefers the surface wording; al-Wāḥidī also reports his 'unless He intends'. Abū Isḥāq supplies an implied preposition and treats an as accusative. Al-Ṭabarasī says the obedience restriction need not ban speech about permissible acts."}, {"id": "18:23/q13/p3", "position": "The exception qualifies the circumstances or time of saying: speak while attaching God's permission.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī prefers this construction and supports ordinary permission with Moses, Shuʿayb, Ishmael, and the Prophet in 18:69, 28:27, 37:102, 48:27."}, {"id": "18:23/q13/p4", "position": "The exception modifies the intended act, allowing God to prevent an otherwise independent act.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī reports this Muʿtazilī account and rejects it, citing Quranic constructions in 6:80, 7:89, and 6:111."}, {"id": "18:23/q13/p5", "position": "The Prophet may announce a promised disclosure only if God first authorizes it.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī rejects this proposed implied object as unsupported and as requiring an unknowable duty."}, {"id": "18:23/q13/p6", "position": "The exception is perpetual, so no future intention may ever be stated.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī rejects this proposal because 11:108, 10:41, and 18:83 attribute future actions to the Prophet and others."}]}

{"id": "18:23/q15", "question": "Why must a future promise be made conditional?", "turns_on": "The notes give complementary grounds: uncertainty about fulfillment and dependence on divine will.", "positions": [{"id": "18:23/q15/p1", "position": "An obstacle or changed circumstances may prevent fulfillment and make an unconditional assertion false or an oath broken.", "reasons": "Al-Māwardī invokes Moses' qualified promise about patience in 18:70; al-Jubbāʾī in al-Ṭabarasī names illness, inability, or changed intention. Al-Qurṭubī and al-Jishumī stress avoiding falsehood; al-Ālūsī says even distant plans face death. Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī reports this rationale for the omitted-saying interpretation but disputes that construction."}, {"id": "18:23/q15/p2", "position": "A person lacks foreknowledge and independent control; God may delay, withhold, or empower the intended act.", "reasons": "Al-Māwardī points to divine power and assistance. Al-Qushayrī says events issue from God's will. Ibn Kathīr says God knows all unseen outcomes and counterfactuals. Elmalılı and Kuran Yolu cite 31:34 about tomorrow's unknown. {"id": "18:23/q16", "question": "What does the verse imply about human agency and God's will?", "turns_on": "Whether agents have efficacy independent of God's enabling will.", "positions": [{"id": "18:23/q16/p1", "position": "People act through power and permission granted by God; they should acknowledge His will rather than claim independent efficacy.", "reasons": "Al-Māwardī says God governs actions by power and assistance; al-Qāshānī says people act through Him. He notes Quranic attribution of actions to people in 10:41 and 28:55 remains valid. Elmalılı and Kuran Yolu cite 31:34 for ignorance of tomorrow."}, {"id": "18:23/q16/p2", "position": "One Muʿtazilī interpretation treats the act as independently caused, with God able to prevent it.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī reports and rejects the reading; he refers to Quranic usage at 6:80, 7:89, and 6:111."}]}
{"id": "18:23/q17", "question": "Must the exception accompany every future claim, including certain outcomes?", "turns_on": "Whether the condition handles only actual contingency or also teaches a general manner of speech.", "positions": [{"id": "18:23/q17/p1", "position": "It applies to possible future events, while a certain event need not receive the same exception.", "reasons": "Al-Jishumī distinguishes contingencies from certainties; he explains the conditional promise of entry to the Sacred Mosque in 48:27 by saying some addressees might die first."}, {"id": "18:23/q17/p2", "position": "It is established practice to qualify every matter, even where God's promised outcome is certain.", "reasons": "Al-Zarkashī uses the promised entry to the Sacred Mosque in 48:27: its fulfillment was certain, but the phrasing teaches the practice commanded here."}]}

{"id": "18:23/q20", "question": "Can a forgotten qualification be supplied later?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "18:23/q20/p1", "position": "Yes; say it upon remembering, even after a long interval.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAbbās in al-Thaʿlabī permits it even after a year; Yaḥyā and Islahi say to say or remember it upon recall.
